# Introduction {#sec-introduction .deo-introduction}

Stress, low mood, worry and exhaustion are among the most widely shared human experiences. People talk about them with friends, colleagues and online communities long before, and often without ever, receiving a diagnosis. When many people describe the same experience in similar words, that shared description becomes a signal worth studying. Long COVID is the clearest recent example: patients named and documented the condition through online communities, and within months it moved from social media into clinical and policy channels, before most formal studies had begun [@callard2021]. This kind of knowledge is easily dismissed. Leaving people out of how knowledge about their own experience is produced has been described as a form of epistemic injustice, meaning a harm done to someone in their capacity as a knower [@okoroji2023]. The starting point of this review is that the collective experience of distress is evidence waiting to be given structure.

The scale of that experience is large, and most of it never reaches health services. Globally, the COVID-19 pandemic was associated with an estimated 53.2 million additional cases of major depressive disorder (an increase of 27.6%) and 76.2 million additional cases of anxiety disorders (an increase of 25.6%) in 2020 alone [@covidmental2021]. In Indonesia, analysis of the 2018 national basic health survey found depression in 5.1% of adolescents aged 15 to 17 and 5.6% of young adults aged 18 to 24 [@suryaputri2022]. The first national adolescent mental health survey found that about one in twenty adolescents aged 10 to 17 had a mental disorder in the previous year, while only about one in fifty had used any service for emotional or behavioural problems [@inamhs2022]. Burnout is similarly widespread. In an online assessment of 4,338 full-time employees in Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Singapore in 2022, 62.9% reported high or very high burnout [@abdulaziz2024], and a meta-analysis estimated burnout in 39% of the public health workforce worldwide [@nagarajan2024]. In Indonesia, a national survey of 3,629 healthcare workers likewise found burnout syndrome in 37.5% [@lamuri2023]. Measures of resilience, the capacity to cope and recover, are rarely collected alongside these measures of distress, so what helps people stay well is even less visible than what harms them. Because most distress does not reach services, data drawn from services describe only a small, unrepresentative part of it.

Conventional research is poorly placed to fill this gap. Questions are usually chosen by researchers or institutions, and members of the public take part mainly by filling in forms. In a regional study that included Indonesia, community members said they did not know how the information they gave was used [@kumar2025]. This matters for the quality of research as well as for fairness. In a longitudinal study of mental health research in England, studies with greater patient involvement were more likely to reach their recruitment targets, although the association does not prove cause [@ennis2013]. Involvement can also go wrong: when lived-experience roles are filled by a small, well-connected group, or when people are asked to share painful experience without fair support and pay, involvement risks "elite capture" and "epistemic exploitation" [@okoroji2023]. Research done on people, rather than with them, therefore risks asking the wrong questions, recruiting the wrong people and losing their trust.

Citizen science offers a different arrangement. In this paper, citizen science means research in which members of the public take part as partners: choosing questions, designing methods, collecting or interpreting data, and sharing results. Participation ranges from contributing data (crowdsourcing) to defining the problem and leading the research (extreme citizen science) [@haklay2013], and the European Citizen Science Association's ten principles describe what good practice looks like [@robinson2018]. In mental health specifically, a systematic review found that citizen scientists with lived experience reported empowerment, social connection and improved wellbeing and self-esteem, and that the main cost was the time and energy the work required [@todowede2023]. Citizen science can also reach scale: a Dutch crowdsourcing study recruited 12,503 members of the public to report both symptoms and personal strengths, and gave each participant personalised feedback in return [@vanderkrieke2016]. Citizen science therefore has the potential to make research on distress and resilience more relevant, larger in scale and more reciprocal.

Indonesia appears ready for this approach but is not yet familiar with it. In a nine-country study, 82.2% of Indonesian respondents had never heard of citizen science, yet 86.3% owned a smartphone and 91.6% had internet access; community support, including mental support, stood out as a way Indonesians wanted to contribute [@tan2024]. During the COVID-19 pandemic, grassroots groups began collecting and publishing health data themselves because official information was inadequate [@nadzir2020], and one such group documented health-worker deaths that no official source was counting [@ekawati2022]. The conditions for phone-based, citizen-centred mental health research exist; the practice does not yet.

The evidence base for that practice has three gaps. First, all nine studies in the systematic review of citizen science in mental health were conducted in high-income countries [@todowede2023]. Second, the same review found that studies rarely reported feedback to citizen scientists and none reported making their data publicly available, so it is hard to judge how projects were actually run [@todowede2023]. Third, failures are rarely written up, which biases lessons toward success. This review addresses these gaps by comparing successful and failed cases on a single scoring framework. It asks three questions: (1) What does citizen involvement look like at each stage of research, from choosing the question to acting on findings? (2) Which initiatives in Indonesia and elsewhere have done this, and what happened? (3) What do these cases teach for building citizen-centred mental health research? It is the first paper in a series: its lessons inform a set of principles for research-ready health data (Paper 2), an assessment of an open-source research platform against those principles (Paper 3), and a baseline study of depression, anxiety, burnout, resilience and functioning among adults in three Indonesian cities (Paper 4).
